Deployment#SYS-01

Production network deployment at hyperscale

New data center capacity has to be cabled, validated and handed to operations before it can carry customer traffic. My work is the step between the engineering design and that handoff.

  • Deploy network infrastructure from engineering runbooks in a spine/leaf architecture
  • Install and validate optical transceivers and patch high-density fiber trunks
  • Review validation results and clear link and port errors until equipment passes
  • Hand off to operations with completed work, open items and next steps documented

Operations#SYS-02

Fault isolation & out-of-band recovery

When a link fails on a live floor, the expensive mistake is guessing. I narrow the problem down from logs and monitoring first, then decide whether it needs a remote fix, a power cycle, or hands on hardware.

  • Read system logs and optical power readings to localize link failures
  • Traced faults through topology diagrams to correct mislabeled or misrouted cabling
  • Safely drained and powered down devices through change tickets, then brought them back up
  • Rebuilt console / out-of-band management devices to restore remote access

04About

Between the design and the live region.

Most people meet the cloud as a console. I meet it as cold aisles, fiber trays and a runbook. My job is the step between an engineering design and a live region: making sure every transceiver seats, every link comes up clean, and every rack reaches operations documented and ready.

I came into IT through the Per Scholas × TEKsystems Data Center program, where I led a seven-person team through a full enterprise network build. Since then I have moved straight onto production hyperscale data center floors, completed CodePath’s Intermediate Cybersecurity program, and kept going on an A.S. in IT. Next up: AWS Solutions Architect Associate.

What I bring: speed without shortcuts, calm troubleshooting on live equipment, and trackers that other people can actually rely on.

CodePath CYB102 · Web app security · 2026

Web app security: exploiting a directory traversal flaw

Scripted an attack on a vulnerable file server that escaped its public folder with URL-encoded ../ paths, read other users’ private reports, and pulled the real earnings figure the app was hiding.

private files read from outside the public folder
3
private files read from outside the public folder
Bash script automating the attack
1
Bash script automating the attack
BashNode.jsDirectory traversalURL encoding
01

The attack running

02

What I did

  • Used %2e%2e (URL-encoded “..”) to step out of /general into other users’ folders: timmy, wanda and cosmo.
  • Wrapped server start-up, the attack path and clean-up in one Bash script, so each test is a one-line change.
03

How it should be fixed

  • Decode and normalize every requested path, then reject anything that resolves outside the public folder.
  • Serve files from an allowlist, and run the server with only the permissions it needs.

01

The case in Catalyst

02

Checking the report’s indicators

IndicatorThe report saidWhat I foundVerdict
MD5 3AADBF7E…Remote access trojanFlagged by ~45 of 60 engines; matches the Valyria/PoetRAT family: a Word macro dropper that runs a Python payloadCONFIRMED
93.184.216.34High-confidence malicious0% abuse score on AbuseIPDB, 1 of 91 vendors on VirusTotal; a CDN address long used for example.comMISLABELED
03

Gaps I found, and what I’d change

01

Unvetted indicators

IssueIOCs went into the report without a reputation check, so a harmless address was marked high-confidence malicious.

FixValidate every IOC automatically before it’s added to a case.

02

Macros allowed

IssueThe chain was link → Word document → macro → Python RAT. Nothing stopped the macro from running.

FixGroup Policy that blocks macros in Office files downloaded from the internet, breaking the chain at its first step.

04

Most important phase

Containment. Even when detection is slow, containing the host quickly stops an attacker from spreading, escalating privileges or taking data.

File integrity monitoring with Linux auditd

Put kernel-level watch rules on sensitive files, let three attack scripts run, and used the audit log to prove exactly which script changed which file.

tampered files detected
4

attack scripts
3

changes traced to the script that made them
4/4

Linuxauditdauditctlausearch
01

Which attack changed which file

FileChanged by
cloudia.txtattack-a
oakley.txtattack-b
squeaky.txtattack-b
precipitation.csvattack-c
02

How it works

  • auditctl -w <file> -p wa -k <key> watches a file for writes and attribute changes, tagged with a search key.
  • The kernel logs every matching system call, so nothing slips past the watch.
  • ausearch -k <key> pulls up only that file’s events, and the comm= field names the process that made the change.

05

How it was built

Switching
  • ✓Separate VLANs for servers and workstations
  • ✓Access ports grouped by VLAN; Gi1/0/24 trunked to the router
  • ✓Unused ports moved to VLAN 99 and shut down
  • ✓SSH management with 2048-bit RSA keys
Routing & edge
  • ✓Router-on-a-stick with subinterfaces for inter-VLAN routing
  • ✓NAT/PAT inside/outside for internet access
  • ✓DHCP pool for the workstation range

Virtualization
  • ✓ESXi vSwitch0 bound to the physical server NIC
  • ✓“Server-Net” port group mapped to the server VLAN
  • ✓Windows Server 2019 VM: 4 vCPU · 8 GB RAM · 80 GB disk
  • ✓VMFS datastore on the local RAID volume
Structured cabling
  • ✓Cat6 UTP, RJ-45, T568B keystone terminations
  • ✓Color-coded: blue servers · yellow workstations · red uplinks
  • ✓Both ends labeled with port and destination
  • ✓Runs within the 100 m TIA-568 limit; 24-port 1U patch panel

Inter-VLAN isolation failed on first run; extended ACLs on the router subinterfaces fixed it before handoff.

09

What broke, and how we fixed it

01

Overlapping subnets

IssueTwo teams sharing the rack picked the same address range, which confused routing.

FixI coordinated all four teams onto one master IP plan, with a separate block for each team.

02

VLAN bleed

IssueThe workstation VLAN could reach the server VLAN without restriction.

FixExtended ACLs on the router subinterfaces allow only the traffic users need, such as RDP and SMB.

03

VM had no network

IssueThe Windows Server VM’s NIC was attached to the wrong ESXi port group.

FixAudited the vSwitch config, moved the NIC to “Server-Net” and re-tested.

04

Trip hazard

IssueFloor runs from the rack to workstations were unsafe.

FixRe-routed along baseboards and secured flush to the wall.

10

Risk register: single points of failure

ComponentImpact if it failsSeverityMitigation
Single switchAll VLAN connectivity lostHIGHSecond switch with spanning tree / link aggregation
Single routerNo internet, no inter-VLAN routingHIGHHSRP/VRRP with a standby router
Single ISP uplinkFull internet outageHIGHDual ISP with BGP or policy-based routing
No UPSUnplanned outages and data lossHIGH1,500 VA UPS with auto-shutdown
Single server NICServer network downMEDNIC teaming on the ESXi host
11

What I’d carry into the next build

  • Agree the IP plan with every party before anyone configures anything. Fixing overlap mid-build is expensive.
  • Cable labels matter as much as configs; unlabeled runs cost us the most troubleshooting time.
  • ESXi virtual networking has to mirror the physical VLAN design exactly.
  • Harden in small steps and test after each one, not all at the end.
  • Add monitoring (SNMP with Zabbix or Nagios) and change management, even in a lab.

CodePath CYB102 · Network forensics · 2026

Network forensics: finding a phishing sender in packet captures

Given four packet captures, found the one machine running a sextortion phishing campaign, using Wireshark display filters to separate it from normal mail traffic.

packet captures analyzed
4
packet captures analyzed
phishing emails sent within seconds
24
phishing emails sent within seconds
sending IP identified
1
sending IP identified
WiresharkPCAP analysisSMTPPhishing analysis
01

How I found it

  • Applied the imf filter (Internet Message Format) to see the actual emails inside each capture.
  • One capture stood out: a single internal IP, 10.6.1.104, sent 24 emails within seconds to different recipients.
  • The sender addresses rotated through random domains, and every subject line used threatening, urgent language: classic sextortion phishing.
  • Confirmed with ip.src == 10.6.1.104, which showed the SMTP traffic going out to an external mail server.
  • The other three captures each held a single legitimate test email.
02

Why it matters

Packet captures are a recording of exactly what crossed the network. Knowing the right filters turns thousands of packets into one clear answer: who sent what, to whom, and when.

The Data Dig: DDoS detection in a software-defined network

A four-person team analyzing a 1,048,575-row DDoS dataset from a simulated software-defined network, and adapting CISA’s DDoS response playbook to how SDN actually works.

rows of labeled traffic
1,048,575
rows of labeled traffic
team members
4
team members
hypotheses to test
3
hypotheses to test
changes to the CISA playbook
5
changes to the CISA playbook
Python (pandas)WiresharkSplunkSnortZeekCISA playbooks
01

My role

  • Researched SDN and the Ryu controller so the team understood where the data came from.
  • Mapped the playbook’s phases to our findings: what detection and containment look like in this network.
  • Co-wrote the playbook adaptation, and own the presentation.
02

What we expect to find

  • Attack traffic will have much higher packet rates and smaller, more uniform packets than normal traffic.
  • A few source IPs will produce most of the traffic during attacks.
  • Delay, jitter and packet loss will rise sharply during attack windows.
03

Adapting CISA’s playbook to SDN

Detect at the controller
  • ✓The controller sees every switch’s flow table
  • ✓Watch for spikes in flows, packet rate and uniform short flows
Contain with flow rules
  • ✓Push drop or rate-limit rules from the controller
  • ✓Network-wide in seconds, instead of edge firewall rules
Thresholds from data
  • ✓Packet-rate and per-source limits taken from our own analysis
  • ✓Replaces generic “unusual volume” wording
Validate against labels
  • ✓Score the playbook’s detection rules against the dataset’s ground truth
  • ✓Drop steps that don’t apply to a lab dataset

CodePath CYB102 · SIEM · 2026

SIEM investigation: tracing a malware upload in Splunk

Solved all 15 Splunk capture-the-flag challenges: ten search drills on a large media dataset, then a five-step investigation that traced a known-bad file hash back to the attacker’s IP, the accounts they tried, the browser they used and the file they planted.

CTF challenges solved

8 min
between the malicious and a legitimate upload
malicious file confirmed by hash
1

SplunkSPLLog analysisIncident timeline
01

The investigation, step by step

  1. Step 101
    Hash to IP

    Searched the MD5 hash of the known malware and found the uploading IP: 192.168.1.10.

  2. Step 202
    IP to accounts

    Login attempts from that IP used ABurke, Admin and Pi. The upload succeeded as ABurke.

  3. Step 303
    Attacker’s browser

    The successful upload came from a Firefox/89.0 user agent.

  4. Step 404
    Rule out noise

    A second upload 8 minutes later came from Jmann at 192.168.1.7: a normal proposal.pdf.

  5. Step 505
    Name the file

    Matching hashes to filenames confirmed EvilScript.exe as the malicious upload.

02

Search techniques used

  • Field filters and wildcards to narrow a dataset to exactly the events that matter.
  • stats count, top, table and sort to turn raw events into answers.
  • Pivoting: each answer (hash, IP, username, time) became the filter for the next search.
03

Takeaway

Timestamps are the most important field in a log. Lining up the two uploads by time is what separated the attack from normal activity, and correlating events by time is the whole point of a SIEM.

What each rule does

Connection limits
  • ✓limit_conn_zone per client IP
  • ✓limit_conn 10: one client can’t hog the server
Rate limiting
  • ✓limit_req at 10 requests per second
  • ✓burst 20 absorbs normal spikes
Timeouts
  • ✓client_header_timeout 5s and client_body_timeout 5s
  • ✓Slow, never-finished requests get dropped
Keep-alive
  • ✓keepalive_timeout 15s, send_timeout 10s
  • ✓Idle connections free up quickly

Threat hunt: SolarWinds and Scattered Spider indicators in Splunk

Took published indicators of compromise from two real-world campaigns and hunted for them in a simulated company’s traffic logs, to find which machines talked to attacker infrastructure, when, and how widely.

SplunkSPLVirusTotalThreat intelligenceIOC hunting
01

How I hunted

  • Loaded each campaign’s IOC list and the company traffic log into Splunk as two sources.
  • Wrote one SPL search that groups events by IP or domain and keeps only values seen in both sources (mvcount(sources) > 1), so only real matches survive.
  • Tabled the computer name, user agent, date and time for every match to build a timeline.
  • Checked each indicator’s reputation in VirusTotal to see how the infrastructure had aged.
02

Scattered Spider: matches in Splunk

05

linkedinsso.comWS-HR-888Sep 15, 09:47

06

What it showed

  • SolarWinds hid inside trusted software updates; Scattered Spider went after people with fake login domains. Two very different ways in.
  • The SolarWinds IPs still carry a malicious reputation years later, while the phishing domains are newer and short-lived. Old indicators are still worth hunting.
  • Two compromises years apart point to a monitoring gap: I’d recommend automatic IOC correlation alerts, domain-based detection and targeted phishing awareness for high-access teams.

Privacy & legal

Privacy policy and legal notices

Effective November 15, 2026

The short version
  • ✓ No cookies, no analytics, no ads, no trackers.
  • ✓ No forms: nothing you type is sent anywhere.
  • ✓ No third-party scripts or fonts are loaded; everything is served from this site.
  • ✓ The only thing stored on your device is your light/dark theme choice.

1. What is collected

This site does not collect personal information. It has no accounts, contact forms, comment boxes, analytics or advertising.

Like every website, the hosting provider automatically processes basic technical data when your browser requests a page: your IP address, browser and device type, the page requested, and the time. This is needed to deliver the site and protect it from abuse (for example, denial-of-service attacks). This site is hosted by Vercel; a copy may also be served by GitHub Pages. Their privacy policies describe how they handle these logs. I don’t use these logs to identify visitors.

2. Cookies and local storage

This site sets no cookies, so there is no cookie banner.

If you switch between light and dark mode, that choice is saved in your browser’s local storage under the name theme. It never leaves your device, contains no personal information, and you can clear it at any time in your browser settings.

3. If you email me

If you contact me by email, I receive your email address and whatever you choose to write. I use it only to reply to you. I don’t sell or share it, add it to mailing lists, or use it for marketing. Ask me and I’ll delete our correspondence.

4. Links to other sites

This site links to my LinkedIn profile. Those links open LinkedIn in a new tab and are covered by LinkedIn’s own privacy policy. Nothing from LinkedIn is embedded or loaded on this site.

5. Your rights

Depending on where you live (for example, under the GDPR in the EU/UK or the CCPA in California), you may have the right to know what personal information I hold about you, to have it corrected or deleted, and to object to its use. Because this site collects no personal information, the only data I could hold is email you sent me. To make a request, email me using the address in the Contact section.

This site is not directed to children under 13, and I don’t knowingly collect information from them.

6. Security

The site is served only over HTTPS and uses a strict Content Security Policy, anti-framing protection and other security headers. If you find a security issue, please report it privately (see security.txt).
